doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Early ear and singing harmony as a child
summary: Marty recalls childhood, his comic brother, his banjo-playing father noting his ear, and singing harmony in school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Can you recall at what age did you think you could actually make a career as a musician? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

I recall every day of my life just about, I swear, all of it. Really. I remember asking my mother a question once, where I said, “Mom, you remember when you were scrubbing the floor in the kitchen?” And she uttered some obscenity about some neighbors or somebody, and I said, “were you talking about me?” She said, “no, honey, not you, no, no, I mean them.” So I said, “how old was I then?” She says, “you were two years old.” And after that she says, “I thought you were going to be a school teacher because I used to stand up and by the time I was three or four years old I used to stand on the chair by the kitchen table, and bang the table, and speak gibberish. She thought I was making speeches, which I was, I was making speeches and banging my fist on the table. So I remember all of these crazy little things you know. But as far as being a musician or a piano player, well the fact is that when I was about seven or eight years old I had a brother who was like four or five years older than I, and he was kind of like a Danny Kaye kind of character, he was crazy, he was like a nut job. He’d do all these crazy motions. And he used to sing like comedy songs. And I used to sing harmony to him. And my father, who was a banjo player, said, “this kid’s got a great ear.” And I had a good ear, because I could hear harmonies at the time I was about seven years old. And when I used to go to grammar school, we’d sit in the auditorium and they’d say “everybody stand up, we’re going to sing the ‘Star Spangled Banner’” and the kids would be singing [sings] Oh say can you see—and I was singing [sings harmony] Oh say can you see, by the dawn’s early light. And the kid next to me says, “hey, you’re singing it wrong.” I says, “shut up, I know what I’m doing.” I was singing counterharmonies. I mean this is what I heard. And the funny thing is, to jump ahead of myself, when I was with the Chico Marx band, one of my first big bands, actually there was band before that was my first big band, but Chico Marx was my first name big band. And we played, you know Chico Marx, the Marx Brothers, and I was on the road with that band for a year and a half. My wife, we had just gotten married and we were on the road, and we were doing mostly only theaters, mostly theaters anyway, and we’d have, each week we were in a different town, and we’d have an eight o’clock rehearsal in the theater and they’d have people like Larry Adler, who is my biggest nightmare because he was playing all these “Rhapsody in Blue” and Ravel’s “Bolero” and I couldn’t read note one.
